drills.q: List the ten LLM-code failure modes in the order this module checks them.
drills.a: Fabricated API/import, deprecated/removed API, silently swallowed errors, missing edge cases, over-abstraction, tests asserting implementation not behavior, plausible-but-wrong concurrency, confidently wrong comments, idiom mismatch, unjustified complexity for scale.

drills.q: Why can't you use "the code reads confidently" as a signal of correctness for AI-generated code?
drills.a: LLM fluency is a token-probability property generated identically for real and hallucinated APIs -- there's no internal signal distinguishing certainty from plausible invention, unlike a human author whose confidence tracks actual certainty.

drills.q: A generated module has 100% test coverage. Explain concretely why this doesn't guarantee the tests catch regressions, and how you'd prove it either way.
drills.a: Coverage measures line execution, not assertion quality -- a test can execute every line while asserting only that a mock was called, which can't fail even against a broken implementation making the same call. Run a mutation-testing tool (mutmut/Stryker/PIT) to deliberately break the implementation and confirm at least one test goes red for each mutation; surviving mutations expose exactly which "covered" lines have no real assertion behind them.

drills.q: Explain the check-then-act concurrency bug: why does a lock in the code not guarantee safety, and why do unit tests typically miss it?
drills.a: A lock acquired around only the check, or only the act, but not both atomically, leaves the combined check-then-act sequence exposed -- two concurrent callers can each pass the check before either performs the act. Unit tests run sequentially by default and essentially never inject real thread interleaving at exactly the check-act boundary, so the bug doesn't manifest until real contention under production load hits that exact timing window.

drills.q: What is slopsquatting and why does it make a hallucinated import a security issue, not just a build failure?
drills.a: Slopsquatting is attackers registering package names LLMs are observed to hallucinate frequently. A build failure only occurs if the fabricated name doesn't exist; once an attacker registers that exact name, the install succeeds and pulls in malicious code -- CI passing on install is not evidence the dependency is legitimate.

drills.q: Rank and justify review priority for a single PR containing: a hallucinated import, an over-engineered factory, a swallowed exception in a payment path, a stale comment, and a mock-only test covering the payment path.
drills.a: 1) Swallowed exception in the payment path -- highest severity, silent money/data corruption. 2) Hallucinated import -- blocks build or resolves to a malicious package. 3) Mock-only test on the payment path -- compounds with #1 since the fix wouldn't actually be verified. 4) Over-abstraction and 5) stale comment -- real but lower severity, non-blocking or same-PR-but-not-urgent.

drills.q: A teammate says increased general attention when reading AI-generated code makes a fixed checklist unnecessary. What's the gap in that argument?
drills.a: General careful reading catches what careful human review has always caught -- typos, obvious logic errors, style issues -- but fabricated-but-plausible API calls, mock-only tests, and check-then-act races don't look wrong on a careful read; they look like ordinary correct code. A checklist forces the specific mechanical checks (import resolution, exception handling, test-assertion quality, concurrency trace) that fluency makes easy to skip, freeing remaining attention for genuine judgment calls like design fit.

drills.q: Why is a comment mismatch in AI-generated code categorically different from typical human comment drift, and what review implication follows?
drills.a: Human comment drift usually starts accurate and goes stale after a later code change, often carrying residual signal (it was true once) and sometimes reading slightly inconsistent as a tell. A generated comment can be wrong from the moment of creation with no prior accurate state, generated with full fluency regardless of match to the code -- so "this comment looks stale" is not a reliable tell here; every behavior-describing comment must be verified against the code directly, not triaged by how old or confident it reads.
